noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand that bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder
understand the role of bile in neutralising stomach acid and emulsifying lipids

primer.text: You have met the stomach's acid and the intestine's enzymes in passing. This short lesson slots bile between them: where the liver makes it, where the gall bladder parks it, and the two jobs — neutralising acid and emulsifying fat — that let the small intestine's enzymes work at their best.

lessons.title: Bile: Made by the Liver, Working in the Gut
lessons.opening: Bile is an alkaline fluid — the liver makes it, the gall bladder stores it — until the small intestine needs it. There it does two jobs at once: it neutralises the acidic chyme arriving from the stomach, and its salts emulsify large fat drops into many tiny ones, multiplying the surface that lipase can attack.
keyPoints: Cells in the liver produce bile, an alkaline substance.
The gall bladder stores bile before release into the small intestine.
Bile neutralises hydrochloric acid arriving from the stomach.
Intestinal enzymes work best at a higher, more alkaline optimum pH.
Emulsification breaks large lipid drops into smaller ones with more surface area.
With alkaline conditions and extra surface, lipase converts lipid to glycerol and fatty acids faster.

low.restatement: Liver makes it, gall bladder stores it, gut benefits twice.
low.analogy: A delivery van: stocked at the depot (gall bladder), unloading where the work is (intestine).
low.examPointer: Name both organs of production and storage — each carries a mark.

medium.restatement: Bile's two roles are physical and chemical setup: neutralise the pH, then multiply the surface for enzymes.
medium.analogy: Preparing a workshop: clean the bench (neutralise), then spread out the parts (emulsify).
medium.examPointer: Remember emulsification is mechanical digestion — no bonds are broken.

check.stem: Which cells in the body make bile?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
The gall bladder only stores it.
The stomach makes acid, not bile.
The pancreas makes enzymes and insulin, not bile.

check.stem: Which molecule actually emulsifies the lipid?

options.text: The bile salts carried in bile
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Lipase splits molecules; salts split drops.
Acid arrives to be neutralised, not to emulsify.
Glycerol is a product, not an agent.

check.stem: Why must stomach acid be neutralised in the small intestine?

options.text: Intestinal enzymes need a more alkaline optimum pH than the stomach's enzymes enjoy
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Acid would dissolve the intestinal wall
options.explanation: Neutralisation is about enzyme pH, not wall damage.
Water absorption is unaffected by the acid directly.
Emulsification works better once acid is neutralised.

check.stem: What does emulsification change about a fat drop?

options.text: It splits one large drop into smaller ones, increasing the surface area
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: It changes the fat into glycerol chemically
options.explanation: That chemical split is lipase's job.

options.text: It raises the fat's melting point
options.explanation: Melting point is untouched.

options.text: It removes the fat from the intestine
options.explanation: The fat stays; only drop size changes.

check.stem: Why is emulsification called mechanical digestion rather than chemical digestion?

options.text: Because breaking drops into pieces changes no bonds or molecular structure
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Bile salts are involved; the distinction is bond-breaking.
Bile is a fluid.

options.text: Because it only happens in the stomach
options.explanation: It happens in the small intestine.

check.stem: State where bile is stored before release.
check.modelAnswer: Bile is stored in the gall bladder before it enters the small intestine.

check.stem: Name the two products of lipid digestion by lipase.
check.modelAnswer: Lipase breaks lipid down into glycerol and fatty acids.

check.stem: Explain why emulsification speeds up lipid digestion.
check.modelAnswer: Because splitting one large drop into many smaller ones multiplies the surface area on which lipase can act, and with alkaline conditions restored the enzyme works at its optimum, so glycerol and fatty acids are released faster.

check.stem: A patient has their gall bladder removed. Predict the consequence for fatty meals.
check.modelAnswer: Without the gall bladder's stored bile, bile still arrives from the liver but not in a concentrated bolus, so large fatty meals are emulsified less effectively and fat digestion proceeds more slowly and less completely.

glossary.definition: The alkaline fluid made by the liver, stored in the gall bladder, that neutralises acid and emulsifies fat.
Breaking large lipid drops into many smaller ones, mechanical digestion that raises surface area.
The acidity at which an enzyme works fastest; intestinal enzymes prefer alkaline conditions.
